fixes.explanation: Ooh, good guess, friend, but nobody asks for a name here. In verse 47 the servant asks, “Whose daughter are you?” Rebekah answers, “The daughter of Bethuel son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.” So he's asking about her family, and only after that do the ring and bracelets go on. I've handed out plenty of cookies without asking a name, but I always know whose kitchen they came from!

Verse 53 says he brought out jewels of silver and gold, and articles of clothing, and gave them to Rebekah. He also gave precious gifts to her brother and her mother. Rebekah's gifts get named first, though. That's a lot of jewels and clothing to carry out of one meeting!

Gifts for her father? Not in this scene, friend. Her brother and mother say, “Let the girl remain with us ten days or so. After that, she may go.” (verse 55). The gifts in this scene go to Rebekah, her brother and her mother (verse 53). What they're asking for is TIME. I get it. When a batch is that good, nobody wants the box to leave the bakery!

Hold on, this one is True. Verse 61 says Rebekah and her servant girls got ready, mounted the camels, and followed the man. So she isn't heading out on her own. I think that's a nice way to set out, with company.

The jar belongs to the spring scene, where she carried it on her shoulder (verse 45). Here, verse 65 says, “So she took her veil and covered herself.” Just before that, she has gotten down from her camel (verse 64) and asked who that man in the field is (verse 65). So no jar this time, just a veil.

A staff? Nope, nobody's walking with a stick in this scene, friend! Rebekah gets down from her camel (verse 64) and asks who the man in the field is. After the servant says, “It is my master…” verse 65 says, “So she took her veil and covered herself.” The veil is the one the text names. I think she wanted to look just right for the moment, and honestly, so would I with my hat on straight.
